title: Which channels carry culture across generations, and why traits fade
text: Unknown is which channel (parents, peers, schools, media, role models, adult experience) carries each trait across generations, and what makes persistence decay or survive once its original economic rationale is gone. Established: traits such as trust, work attitudes and food tastes persist among migrants and descendants, and formal transmission models (Bisin-Verdier, Doepke-Zilibotti) predict how, but their group-size and endogamy predictions have only suggestive tests.
why: Persistence is inferred from correlations of ancestry or origin with outcomes, which cannot separate cultural transmission from continuing economic, geographic or institutional conditions.

title: Whether religious and supernatural beliefs cause cooperation, and how
text: Unknown is whether religious beliefs, rituals and moralizing gods causally raise prosocial and cooperative behaviour, which content or costly signal does the work, and whether in-group gains are offset by out-group discrimination, conflict and stigma. Established: lab and field work shows framing and priming effects on giving, correlations between punitive gods, cultural tightness and social complexity, and some cases of religious institutions managing common resources, mostly for major world religions and WEIRD samples.
why: Effects are shown in narrow samples and by correlation, and historical religion codings are too coarse to test the moralizing-god and complexity link or to separate in-group favouritism from out-group discrimination.

title: What sustains costly religious practice and how religious groups adapt
text: Unknown is what drives people to adopt and keep religious practice, why economically costly fasts, festival timings and sacrifices persist, and how religious organisations adjust teachings and services as costs, competition and ecology change. Established: practice responds to economic costs, trade and ecological conditions in several settings (Ramadan, Catholic festivals, Muslim adherence, religious competition and Islamism), but mostly through static comparisons of more and less religious places.
why: Surveys measure adherence coarsely and statically and exogenous variation in the cost or supply of religion is rare, so demand, self-control and coordination explanations of costly practice cannot be told apart.

title: Whether inherited kinship and moral systems still bind institutions
text: Unknown is whether kinship tightness, moral universalism, trust and collectivism are causal constraints on today's state capacity, finance and democratization, or merely selected by the places and lifestyles that produced them. Established: these traits correlate strongly with ancestral agriculture, lineage organization and historical institutions, and with financial development, trade and political attitudes, but the mechanism from distant history to current institutions is mostly asserted.
why: Culture is slow-moving, almost never randomly assigned and entangled with selection into locations and with the institutions it is meant to explain, so effects of exposure cannot be cleanly separated from sorting.

title: Which levers shift entrenched norms, beliefs and trust durably
text: Unknown is which levers (information correcting misperceived norms, new laws, integrated institutions, culturally matched implementers, narratives about government) change deep norms, beliefs and trust, how fast, for whom, and whether they travel beyond the study setting. Established: misperceptions about others' norms and about marriage-market preferences are common and correctable, law and exposure can shift behaviour, and trust in medicine and government falls after shocks, but few studies track durability or compare delivery designs.
why: Most evidence is a single intervention in one country with short follow-up, and cultural context shapes efficacy in ways not intuitive ex ante, so general lessons are hard to extract.

title: Which contact and institutions defuse diversity's costs and bias
text: Unknown is which forms of contact (schools, sports leagues, neighbourhoods) and which national, local and informal institutions let diverse societies avoid weaker public goods, segregation and discrimination, and how group identities themselves form and should be measured. Established: ethnic diversity is linked to weaker collective action and public goods, contact raises cooperation or shifts attitudes in specific settings, and correspondence studies document discrimination but not its magnitude or institutional channels.
why: Diversity, segregation and identity are endogenous, cross-country segregation and individual identity data are poor, and field designs typically cover one minority in one country.

title: Economic loss or cultural threat behind trade and immigration voting
text: Unknown is how much of the populist and far-right vote after trade, automation and immigration shocks reflects material loss versus cultural or status threat, through which channels (labour competition, welfare access, neighbourhood amenities, group status, financial exposure), and why natural left constituencies do not demand redistribution instead. Established: import competition, refugee arrivals and reception centres raise radical-right support in several European and US settings, but the evidence is mostly aggregate vote shares.
why: Studies regress attitudes on attitudes or use aggregate vote shares and local survey samples that are too thin, so economic and identity channels are not separated.

title: How voter and firm demands become immigration and emigration policy
text: Unknown is when mass-public hostility or firm and interest-group preferences win in setting immigration policy, how this works beyond rich democracies and over the long run, and why autocracies use emigration as a safety valve or control tool. Established: trade exposure, production location and natural resources shape firms' immigration preferences, policy closedness is now measured for rich democracies, and emigration opportunities deter some recruitment into violent movements, but trade, immigration and emigration are studied separately.
why: Cross-national and historical data on migration policy were scarce until recently, and policy is rarely observed in the Global South or in non-democracies.

title: Whether partisan identity distorts economic decisions: taste or belief
text: Unknown is whether political identity changes the decisions of firms, investors, workers and consumers through taste (favouring copartisans) or through biased beliefs (team-fan optimism, belief disagreement), how large the aggregate cost is, and how far it spreads to other professions and countries. Established: partisan alignment shifts perceptions, capital allocation, hiring, patenting productivity and regional entrepreneurship after elections, mostly in the US and in survey or single-sector settings.
why: Taste-based and belief-based discrimination are observationally very close, and most designs rely on survey experiments or one election episode rather than field or firm-level variation in political losses.

title: Whether who runs and wins (identity, party, primaries) changes policy
text: Unknown is whether the identity, party and selection of office-holders causally changes policy, through what mechanism (taste, strategic extremism, career incentives, primary voters), and why platforms diverge from the median when voters are uncertain about candidates. Established: partisan control and legislators' family characteristics shift local policy and votes in several quasi-experiments, and signalling and primary models predict divergence, but direct tests of these mechanisms are rare.
why: Quasi-experiments identify a local effect of office-holding but cannot separate preference change from cost or constituency changes, and data on the pool of potential candidates and on later party careers are missing.

title: What drives polarization and how to measure ideology beyond Congress
text: Unknown is which factors cause the rise in partisan and affective polarization and the transformation of political cleavages (political supply, sorting, media and language, agenda and replacement effects), whether deliberation or other designs reduce it, and how to measure ideology of non-incumbents, donors, agencies and legislators outside the US. Established: partisan language, sorting and affective animus have risen in the US, roll-call scaling gives one-dimensional ideal points, and cross-country harmonized series exist for few countries.
why: Cross-country trend data cannot reach causal explanations, and roll-call methods assume sincere voting, one dimension and few observations per member, so they cannot scale actors who never vote or vote rarely.

title: Which electoral and legislative rules move policy, and why they exist
text: Unknown is which finer rule details (thresholds, veto and dissolution rules, amendment and recognition procedures, committee assignment, list structure) drive policy and performance, through which channel, and why countries choose or vary them. Established: majoritarian versus proportional systems and presidential versus parliamentary forms are associated with differences in spending, corruption and welfare programmes, and legislative bargaining theory makes sharp predictions about proposal power, but only reduced-form effects and a few tests exist.
why: Cross-country data cannot isolate the causal effect of one rule, institutions are chosen endogenously (and shaped by their history), and empirical measures of separation of powers, cohesion and procedure are missing.

title: Why redistribution does not track inequality, outside rich democracies
text: Unknown is why democracies redistribute less than rising inequality predicts (wealthy capture, differential turnout, partisanship, mobilization of the poor, diffuse versus organised interests), which direction causation runs between inequality and politics, and what drives welfare and inequality trends in authoritarian and developing countries. Established: top-income and wealth series now exist for several rich countries, China and Russia, and partisanship and electoral systems correlate with redistribution, but the causal pathways and non-OECD patterns remain poorly explained.
why: Inequality and politics are jointly determined, capture lacks a cross-nationally usable metric, and long-run comparable distribution and social-protection data are weak outside the rich democracies.

title: How firm, sector and mass preferences become trade and FDI policy
text: Unknown is how the preferences of firms (by size, productivity and global production role), occupations, sectors and mass publics are aggregated into trade, investment and industrial policy, why many import-competing firms back liberalisation while protection persists, and what regime type adds. Established: factor, sector and exporter-importer cleavages explain some tariff and FDI politics, mass trade attitudes are structured, and regime type and country risk correlate with FDI inflows, but the link from preferences to outcomes is largely assumed.
why: Sector and district exposure measures are coarse, firm-level data and theory are only now arriving, and cross-national FDI restriction data were absent until recently.

title: Why similar countries pick different monetary, fiscal and debt regimes
text: Unknown is which domestic political conditions lead governments to choose a peg, independent central bank, fiscal rule or default, why similar economies end up with very different debt and exchange-rate policies, and how domestic and international sources enter the same model. Established: electoral cycles, polarisation, partisanship, interest groups and homeowners shape exchange-rate and fiscal choices, and theory predicts fiscal-rule design and sovereign borrowing credibility, but the models remain static or country-case based.
why: Studies treat monetary, trade and financial policy separately, rely on stylised assumptions such as full capital mobility, and lack data on creditor communities, fiscal-rule enforcement and policy combinations.

title: Whether treaties, institutions and foreign influence change behaviour
text: Unknown is whether international treaties, investment arbitration, trade agreements and foreign interventions (aid, covert action, cyber, geopolitical rivalry) actually change state behaviour, conflict and domestic politics, and for whom, once strategic selection into commitments is accounted for. Established: commitments and foreign actors correlate with compliance, conflict, democratisation and investment, with some natural-experiment evidence, but the counterfactuals are unobserved and covert influence is poorly measured.
why: States select into agreements and receive interventions strategically, secretive intervention data are scarce, and theories of foreign influence and international institutions remain compartmentalised.
